title: Given a number of tasks and prerequisite pairs, enumerate every valid order in which all tasks can be completed. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern combines with backtracking, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: All Tasks Scheduling Orders (Enumerate Every Valid Completion Order)

s1_definition.profdef: All Tasks Scheduling Orders extends the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking to list every valid topological order rather than just one. At each step we try every task currently with in-degree zero, recurse after placing it, and then undo the choice to explore alternatives. The number of orders can be large, so this is exponential in the worst case.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to see all the different legal sequences for running a small set of dependent audit steps, so reviewers can choose the one that fits their staffing. All Tasks Scheduling Orders lists every sequence that respects the prerequisites.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each step branch on every zero in-degree task, recurse, then undo to find all orders.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** All Tasks Scheduling Orders extends the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking to list every valid topological order rather than just one. At each step we try every task currently with in-degree zero, recurse after placing it, and then undo the choice to explore alternatives. The number of orders can be large, so this is exponential in the worst case.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to see all the different legal sequences for running a small set of dependent audit steps, so reviewers can choose the one that fits their staffing. All Tasks Scheduling Orders lists every sequence that respects the prerequisites.

**One line to remember:** At each step branch on every zero in-degree task, recurse, then undo to find all orders.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep the adjacency list and a mutable in-degree array. The recursion maintains the partial order built so far. At each level we scan for every task that currently has in-degree zero and is not yet used, and for each such task we add it to the partial order, decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, and recurse. After the recursion returns we undo those changes by removing the task and restoring the neighbours' in-degrees, which lets us try a different task at this level. When the partial order contains all tasks we record a complete order.

The recursion is `void build(partial, indeg, adj, used, results) { if (partial.size() == n) { results.add(copy(partial)); return; } for each task t with indeg[t]==0 and not used: { use t; for next in adj[t] indeg[next]--; partial.add(t); build(...); partial.removeLast(); for next in adj[t] indeg[next]++; unuse t; } }`. A concrete check: tasks zero before two and one before two give two orders, zero one two and one zero two. Senior nuance: this is exponential because the count of topological orders can be factorial, so it is only practical for small graphs, and it combines the in-degree idea from Kahn's algorithm with classic backtracking.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a small set of dependent audit steps and reviewers want to see every legal sequence so they can pick the one that best fits their staffing on a given day. Only listing one order hides the alternatives. This is exactly how All Tasks Scheduling Orders works: it combines the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking to enumerate every valid sequence.

The code defines an `AuditOrdersService` exposing `allOrders(taskCount, prerequisites)` returning a list of all valid orders. A `Demo` builds a small prerequisite set and logs the number of orders and the orders themselves.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three audit steps with prerequisites that step zero precedes step two and step one precedes step two. We want every valid order.

Step 1 — We build the in-degrees: step zero has zero, step one has zero, and step two has two from steps zero and one.

Step 2 — At the first level both step zero and step one have in-degree zero, so there are two branches to explore.

Step 3 — Taking step zero first, we decrement step two to one, then at the next level only step one is runnable, so we place it, dropping step two to zero, and finally place step two, giving the order zero one two.

Step 4 — We undo back to the top and take step one first, which by the same reasoning yields the order one zero two.

Step 5 — No other first choices exist because step two can never start before its two prerequisites, so the two complete orders are zero one two and one zero two. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:48:02 PM com.bank.auditord.service.AuditOrdersService allOrders
INFO: Found 2 valid audit orders
Oct 27, 2026 9:48:02 PM com.bank.auditord.AuditOrdersApplication main
INFO: All valid audit orders: [[0, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tasks=3, prereqs = 0→2, 1→2
    │
    ▼
  in-degrees: t0=0, t1=0, t2=2
    │
    ├─ branch: place 0 → t2=1 → place 1 → t2=0 → place 2 → [0,1,2]
    │     (undo)
    └─ branch: place 1 → t2=1 → place 0 → t2=0 → place 2 → [1,0,2]
    ▼
  Output: [[0,1,2], [1,0,2]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
All Tasks Scheduling Orders extends the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking so that instead of returning a single order I enumerate every valid order. I keep the adjacency list and a mutable in-degree array, and the recursion carries the partial order built so far. At each level I look for every task that currently has in-degree zero and has not been used, because each of those is a legitimate next choice.

For each runnable task I place it, decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, and recurse, and critically I undo those changes afterward by removing the task and restoring the in-degrees so I can try a different task at the same level. When the partial order holds all tasks I record a complete order. Because the number of valid topological orders can be factorial, this is exponential in the worst case, so I stress that it is only practical for small dependency graphs.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a small set of dependent audit steps where reviewers wanted to see every legal sequence so they could pick the one that fit their staffing on a given day. I ran the in-degree backtracking to enumerate all orders. Explaining that I branch on every runnable task, undo each choice to explore alternatives, and that the count can blow up factorially is what shows an interviewer I understand how the Topological Sort pattern combines with backtracking.
